p.src: Once the troops had been assigned, at daybreak each commander set out in order, and the army began its march that very day. Only the deputy strategist Gongsun Sheng and the three commanders Liu Tang, Zhu Tong, and Mu Hong—four commanders in all—remained to lead the cavalry and infantry and defend the mountain stronghold. The three passes and the water stockade were naturally defended by Li Jun and the others, but that need not be told.

p.src: Now Suo Chao was stationed in the stronghold at Flying Tiger Ravine when a courier came racing up like a shooting star and reported, “Song Jiang’s army, great and small, is beyond counting. It is only twenty or thirty li from the stronghold and will soon be here.” Hearing this, Suo Chao sent an urgent report to Li Cheng at the stronghold on Locust-Tree Slope. Li Cheng, on hearing the news, sent a mounted messenger into the city while preparing his own warhorse, then rode straight to the forward stronghold. Suo Chao received him and related every detail. At the fifth watch the next morning they cooked their meal; at daybreak they struck camp and advanced to Yujia, where they drew up fifteen thousand soldiers and horsemen in battle formation. Li Cheng and Suo Chao, fully armed and armored, reined in their warhorses beneath the commander’s banner. Looking east across the plain, they saw dust rising far away as more than five hundred men came racing toward them. Li Cheng pointed with the tip of his whip, and the soldiers set their feet against the heavy crossbows and drew their powerful bows. The heroes of Liangshan Marsh formed a single battle line at Yujia. There could be seen:

p.src: Every man wore a madder-red kerchief; each was clad alike in a scarlet padded jacket. Gaiters were bound tight on their heron-shanked legs; belly bands were cinched firm around their tiger-and-wolf waists. Three-pronged forks thrust forth a wintry gleam; four-edged maces trailed a chilling mist. Willow-leaf spears and flame-tipped spears stood thick as hemp; bronze blades and crescent-moon sabers swirled like snow. Across the earth red banners billowed like flames; high in the air crimson standards shone with the radiance of sunset clouds.

p.src: From the eastern formation a hero rode to the fore. It was Li Kui, the “Black Whirlwind.” With an axe in each hand, his strange eyes bulging and his hard teeth clenched, he roared, “Do you know the hero of Liangshan Marsh called the Black Whirlwind?” Li Cheng looked down from his horse and laughed with Suo Chao. “Every day we hear talk of the heroes of Liangshan Marsh, yet they are nothing but filthy brigands like these—not worth mentioning! Vanguard, do you see him? Why not capture that rogue first?” Suo Chao laughed. “Why use an ox-cleaver to kill a chicken? One of our fighting officers can win the honor; our commander need not concern himself.” Before he had finished speaking, one of Suo Chao’s officers, Wang Ding by name, came from behind his horse. Brandishing a long spear, he led one hundred cavalrymen in a furious charge. For all Li Kui’s surpassing courage, even with armor protecting his body he could not withstand a cavalry charge, and his men scattered in every direction. Suo Chao led his troops in pursuit past Yujia, but suddenly gongs and drums thundered behind the hillside, and two columns of soldiers burst forth. Xie Zhen and Kong Liang came from the left, Kong Ming and Xie Bao from the right, each pair leading five hundred men into the attack. Only when Suo Chao saw that the enemy had reinforcements was he alarmed. He abandoned the pursuit, reined about, and returned. Li Cheng asked, “Why did you not bring back the rogue?” Suo Chao replied, “I pursued him beyond the hill and was just about to seize him when those scoundrels’ reinforcements appeared. Their ambush troops rose all at once, making it impossible to strike.” Li Cheng said, “Why fear brigands such as these?” He then led every soldier of the forward division charging past Yujia. Ahead, banners waved and men shouted; drums boomed and gongs rang as yet another column of troops appeared. At their head rode a woman warrior, splendidly arrayed. A lyric to the tune “Niannu Jiao” bears witness:

p.src: Skin pure as jade and snow, a face like lotus blossom, endowed with natural grace. Golden armor glitters as its scales stir; a silver-threaded crimson band binds her brow. In slender, jade-white hands she holds twin precious blades. How glorious her heroism! Her autumn-bright eyes glance about, and myriad charms invite the plucking. She gallops her fine steed boldly at the fore, her frost-bright blades swift as wind, intent on hewing down the government troops. Dust flies across her fair face; sweat soaks her battle robe; killing spirit surges through her breast. Warriors lose their souls and foes their courage: among woman generals she stands peerless. Returning victorious, a faint smile blossoms upon both cheeks.

p.src: Now Hu Sanniang led this force beneath a red banner bearing in gold the great words “Woman General Ten-Foot Green Serpent.” Gu Dasao was on her left and Sun Erniang on her right. They commanded more than a thousand soldiers, men of every height and build gathered from mountains in every quarter. Li Cheng looked upon them and said, “What use can soldiers like these be? Vanguard, advance and meet the enemy while I divide the troops and encircle these brigands on every side.” Suo Chao received the order, gripped his gold-dipped axe, spurred his mount, and charged forward. The “Ten-Foot Green Serpent” reined about and fled toward a hollow in the hills. Li Cheng divided his troops and pursued the enemy in every direction. In the midst of the chase, shouts suddenly shook the earth and mist veiled the sky as a column of troops came after them with the speed of flight. Li Cheng hurriedly withdrew fourteen or fifteen li, unable to keep his head and tail together. Just as he retreated into Yujia, Xie Zhen and Kong Liang burst out from the left, leading their men in pursuit and attack; from the right, Kong Ming and Xie Bao burst forth with their troops and likewise fell upon them. The three woman generals wheeled their horses and attacked from behind, scattering Li Cheng’s army in utter disorder. As they urgently sought to regain their stronghold, Li Kui, the “Black Whirlwind,” blocked the way at the fore. Li Cheng and Suo Chao broke through the surrounding troops and seized a road of escape. By the time they regained the stronghold, they had suffered a crushing defeat. Song Jiang’s army did not pursue. Instead, it recalled its troops to rest for a while and established a camp.

p.src: Li Cheng and Suo Chao hurriedly sent a man into the city to inform Grand Secretary Liang, who that very night ordered Wen Da to lead his own troops swiftly forth as reinforcements. Li Cheng received him, and they discussed a plan for driving back the enemy within the stronghold on Locust-Tree Slope. Wen Da laughed. “This is no more than a touch of the mange—hardly worth troubling over! Though I, Wen, possess little talent, tomorrow I shall decide matters in one battle and ensure a complete victory.” That night they settled their plans and issued orders to the soldiers: cook at the fourth watch, don armor at the fifth, and advance at daybreak. After three rolls of the war drums, they struck camp and all advanced to Yujia. Already they saw Song Jiang’s army bearing down upon them like a raging gale. There could be seen:

p.src: Clouds of war drift slowly through the clear sky; clouds of dust spread thickly, obscuring east and west. A hundred thousand valiant warriors shake the earth with their cries; the carriage-mounted cannon thunder like a storm. War drums boom and shake the mountain valleys; banners snap and whip in the winds of heaven. Spear-shadows shake the heavens like leaping white serpents; sword-light dazzles the sun like soaring azure dragons. The six divisions soar like eagles, making ghosts and gods weep; the three armies are as brave as bears and tigers. Stars of Strength and Slaughter have descended to the mortal world; Tianpeng and the divine warriors have left the azure vault. Silver helmets and golden armor gleam like ice and snow; stout bows and powerful crossbows are truly hard to withstand. Every man desires only to fulfill loyalty and honor; they capture kings and behead generals without seeking reward. Broadsword Wen Da knows not his own measure; his wild boasts and vaunted skill are mere petty tricks! In Flying Tiger Ravine troops rise on every side, swift as stars and lightning, with none able to withstand their charge. They shut the pass and gather up their battered arms and armor, fleeing like startled hares to hide among the reeds.

His green-trimmed war boots bore cloud designs; a bright phoenix-winged helmet flashed in the sun, and a jeweled lion belt hung at his waist. In his hand he brandished a wolf-toothed mace; seldom was so awe-inspiring a hero seen.

p.src: Qin Ming reined in his horse and shouted sternly, “Listen, you corrupt officials of Beijing! We have long wished to attack this city, but truly feared bringing harm upon its innocent people. Hand over Lu Junyi and Shi Xiu without trouble, and send out the adulterous woman and her paramour with them; then I shall withdraw my troops and cease battle, and I swear never to trespass against you! But if you stubbornly refuse to see reason, then fire shall rise on Kunlun's heights and consume jade and stone alike—and that doom is close at hand. If you have anything to say, speak quickly and do not delay.” Before he had finished, Wen Da flew into a rage and asked his leading officers, “Who will capture this villain for me?” Before the words had left his mouth, bells jingled behind him and a great general spurred out first. And how was he arrayed?

A magpie-painted bow lay within its case, and wolf-toothed arrows filled his quiver. His dappled dragon-steed stood steady beneath its carved saddle, while he toyed with a great axe in his hands.

p.src: This was Suo Chao, one of Beijing's foremost generals. Because of his impetuous nature, everyone called him the Impatient Vanguard. Riding before the lines, he shouted, “You were an officer appointed by the imperial court. In what way has the state wronged you? Instead of remaining an honorable man, you fled to the wilderness and became a bandit! When I seize you today, I shall hack your corpse into ten thousand pieces; even death cannot atone for your crimes.” Qin Ming was himself another hot-tempered man. Hearing these words was like heaping charcoal into a furnace and pouring oil upon flames. He slapped his horse forward, swung his wolf-toothed mace, and charged straight at him. Suo Chao spurred his horse and drove straight at Qin Ming. The two fierce steeds met, the two weapons rose together, and the assembled troops roared. They fought for more than twenty bouts without either gaining the advantage. Then Han Tao emerged from the vanguard of Song Jiang's army. Still mounted, he took up his bow and nocked an arrow. Waiting until Suo Chao drew close enough, he loosed with a whistle. The arrow struck Suo Chao squarely in the left arm. Dropping his great axe, Suo Chao wheeled his horse and fled toward his own lines. Song Jiang pointed with the tip of his whip, and the whole army, officers and men alike, swept forward to the attack. They slew until corpses covered the countryside and blood flowed in rivers; the enemy suffered a crushing defeat. They pursued them beyond the Yu family settlement and immediately seized the small stockade at Pagoda Tree Slope. That evening Wen Da fled straight to Flying Tiger Ravine. When he counted his troops, one man in three was gone. Song Jiang stationed his forces inside the stockade at Pagoda Tree Slope. Wu Yong said, “The defeated soldiers have fled, and their hearts must be filled with fear. If we do not pursue them while we have the advantage, I fear they will recover their courage, and then haste will avail us nothing.” Song Jiang said, “The military counselor speaks most wisely.” He immediately issued orders: that very night the elite officers and victorious troops were divided into four columns, which set out under cover of darkness and drove toward the city.

p.src: Now Wen Da, having fled to Flying Tiger Ravine, was as frantic as a homeless cur and as desperate as a fish escaped from the net. As he was discussing plans inside the stockade, a junior officer came to report, “A line of fires has appeared on the nearby hills!” Wen Da led out his troops and mounted to investigate. He saw countless torches upon the eastern hills, their light staining every mountain and field crimson. Wen Da led his troops forward to meet the enemy, but cavalry arrived from behind the hills as well. At their head came Little Li Guang, Hua Rong, leading his lieutenants Yang Chun and Chen Da in a sweeping charge. Caught unprepared, Wen Da led his troops back toward Flying Tiger Ravine. Countless torches now appeared on the western hills. At their head, Double Whips Huyan Zhuo led his lieutenants Ou Peng and Yan Shun in a fierce assault. Then battle cries rose behind them. It was Thunderbolt Qin Ming, leading his lieutenants Han Tao and Peng Qi in a concerted attack. Wen Da's forces fell into utter confusion, uprooting the entire camp in their flight. Ahead, battle cries rose yet again amid flickering firelight. It was Heaven-Shaking Thunder Ling Zhen, who had led his assistants by a side path around to the far side of Flying Tiger Ravine and now opened fire with his cannon. Wen Da led his troops in forcing a way through and fled toward the city. But at the sound of drums ahead, a strong body of troops was already blocking the road. From the massed firelight sprang Leopard Head Lin Chong, the commanding general, leading his lieutenants Ma Lin and Deng Fei to bar the way back. War drums thundered on every side and raging fires rose in competition. The soldiers scattered in confusion, each seeking to save his own life. Brandishing his broadsword, Wen Da hacked open a path and escaped. He happened upon Li Cheng, joined forces with him, and retreated while fighting. By the time they had fought until dawn, they had reached the foot of the city walls. When Grand Secretary Liang heard the news, all three souls and seven spirits nearly deserted him in terror. He hastily mustered troops outside the city to receive the shattered survivors, then shut the gates tight and held fast without venturing forth. The next day Song Jiang's forces pursued them, pitched camp directly outside the eastern gate, and prepared to attack the city.

u.src: Now Wen Da, having fled to Flying Tiger Ravine, was as frantic as a homeless cur and as desperate as a fish escaped from the net.
As he was discussing plans inside the stockade, a junior officer came to report, “A line of fires has appeared on the nearby hills!”
Wen Da led out his troops and mounted to investigate. He saw countless torches upon the eastern hills, their light staining every mountain and field crimson.
Wen Da led his troops forward to meet the enemy, but cavalry arrived from behind the hills as well.
At their head came Little Li Guang, Hua Rong, leading his lieutenants Yang Chun and Chen Da in a sweeping charge.
Caught unprepared, Wen Da led his troops back toward Flying Tiger Ravine.
Countless torches now appeared on the western hills.
At their head, Double Whips Huyan Zhuo led his lieutenants Ou Peng and Yan Shun in a fierce assault.
Then battle cries rose behind them. It was Thunderbolt Qin Ming, leading his lieutenants Han Tao and Peng Qi in a concerted attack.
Wen Da's forces fell into utter confusion, uprooting the entire camp in their flight.

Ahead, battle cries rose yet again amid flickering firelight. It was Heaven-Shaking Thunder Ling Zhen, who had led his assistants by a side path around to the far side of Flying Tiger Ravine and now opened fire with his cannon.
Wen Da led his troops in forcing a way through and fled toward the city.
But at the sound of drums ahead, a strong body of troops was already blocking the road.
From the massed firelight sprang Leopard Head Lin Chong, the commanding general, leading his lieutenants Ma Lin and Deng Fei to bar the way back.
War drums thundered on every side and raging fires rose in competition. The soldiers scattered in confusion, each seeking to save his own life.
Brandishing his broadsword, Wen Da hacked open a path and escaped. He happened upon Li Cheng, joined forces with him, and retreated while fighting.
By the time they had fought until dawn, they had reached the foot of the city walls.

u.src: When Grand Secretary Liang heard the news, all three souls and seven spirits nearly deserted him in terror. He hastily mustered troops outside the city to receive the shattered survivors, then shut the gates tight and held fast without venturing forth.
The next day Song Jiang's forces pursued them, pitched camp directly outside the eastern gate, and prepared to attack the city.

p.src: Now Grand Secretary Liang assembled his men at the Defender's Office to confer, but they could find no means of relief. Li Cheng said, “The bandit army is at the walls, and the danger is urgent. If we delay, the city will surely fall. Your Excellency should write an urgent family letter and send a trusted man to ride through the night to the capital. He must inform Grand Preceptor Cai, so that Cai may promptly petition the court to dispatch elite troops to our relief. This is the best plan. Second, send urgent official dispatches to the neighboring prefectures and counties, ordering them also to muster troops quickly and come to our aid. Third, within Beijing, order Daming Prefecture to conscript laborers and send them atop the walls to assist with one accord in defending the city. Prepare rolling logs and catapult stones, trigger-fired crossbows and powerful bows, jars of lime and boiling filth, and stand watch day and night. Thus we may remain secure.” Grand Secretary Liang said, “The family letter can readily be written, but who will make the journey?” That very day Commander Wang Ding was chosen. Fully armed and accompanied by several cavalrymen, he received the secret letter. The city gate and drawbridge were opened to let him out, and he sped toward the eastern capital to report the situation. Dispatches were also sent to neighboring prefectures, calling upon them to send troops to the rescue. First, Prefect Wang was ordered to muster laborers and station them atop the walls for the defense. No more need be said of that. Meanwhile Song Jiang assigned his generals and led his troops in surrounding the city. They pitched camps on the eastern, western, and northern sides, leaving only the southern gate uninvested. Each day he led his troops in attacking one side of the city. He pressed the mountain stronghold to send provisions, planning for a prolonged encampment. He was determined to break Beijing and rescue Squire Lu and Shi Xiu. For several days Li Cheng and Wen Da led troops out of the city to give battle, but could win no victory. Suo Chao was still recuperating from his arrow wound and had not yet recovered.

p.src: We shall say no more for now of Song Jiang’s forces attacking the city. Meanwhile, the chief officer Wang Ding bore the secret letter and, with three horsemen, rode straight to the Grand Preceptor’s residence in the Eastern Capital, where he dismounted before the gate. The gatekeeper sent word inside, and the Grand Preceptor ordered Wang Ding admitted. He went directly to the rear hall, made his obeisance, and presented the secret letter. Grand Preceptor Cai broke the seal and read the letter. Greatly alarmed, he asked for all the particulars. Wang Ding recounted everything concerning Lu Junyi, point by point. “Song Jiang has now surrounded the city with his army. His might is overwhelming, and we cannot withstand him.” He also related in full the fighting at the Yu estate, Sophora Tree Slope, and Flying Tiger Ravine. Cai Jing said, “You are weary from your hard ride. Go and lodge at the posthouse for now, while I summon the officials to deliberate.” Wang Ding submitted once more, “Your Excellency, Grand Preceptor, Daming is as precarious as a pile of eggs and may fall at any moment. If it should be lost, what is to become of the prefectures and counties north of the Yellow River? I beg Your Excellency to dispatch troops without delay and wipe them out!” Cai Jing said, “Say no more. Withdraw for now.” Wang Ding departed. The Grand Preceptor at once sent a steward of his household to summon the officials of the Bureau of Military Affairs for urgent deliberations on this grave military crisis. Before long, Tong Guan, Commissioner of Military Affairs in the Eastern Hall, arrived at the council chamber with the grand commandants of the Three Commands, and they paid their respects to the Grand Preceptor. Cai Jing explained the peril facing Daming in full, then said, “What stratagem shall we now employ, and what able commander can drive back the bandits and preserve the city?” When he had finished, the assembled officials looked at one another, fear written on every face. Then a man stepped out from behind the Grand Commandant of the Infantry Command. He was Xuan Zan, a defensive commissioner holding the merit title Baoyi, and had charge of troops and horses. His face was black as the bottom of a pot, his nostrils turned upward, and he had curling hair and a red beard. He stood eight feet tall with a tigerish frame, wielded a steel saber, and possessed outstanding martial skill. He had once served as a prince’s son-in-law and was known as the Ugly Prince’s Consort. He had defeated a foreign general in a contest of rapid-fire archery, and the prince, admiring his martial prowess, had taken him as his son-in-law. But who could have imagined that the princess, repelled by his ugliness, would pine away in resentment and die? For this reason he was never entrusted with high office and attained only the post of Baoyi Commissioner of Troops and Horses. Tong Guan was a sycophantic flatterer; he and Xuan Zan could not tolerate one another and had long harbored mutual suspicion. At that moment, unable to contain himself, Xuan Zan stepped out from the ranks and submitted to the Grand Preceptor, “In former days I had an acquaintance in my native district. He is a direct descendant of Guan Yu, the Loyal and Valiant King of Martial Peace from the tripartite age at the end of the Han. His surname is Guan and his given name is Sheng. In bearing he resembles his ancestor Yunchang, and he wields a Green Dragon Crescent Blade; men call him Guan Sheng the Great Blade. He presently serves as patrol inspector of Pudong, languishing in a lowly post. From childhood he studied the military classics, and he is deeply versed in martial arts, with valor enough to withstand ten thousand men. If he is invited with proper ceremony and gifts and appointed commander-in-chief, he can sweep the stronghold from the marsh, annihilate those mad rebels, safeguard the realm, and bring peace to the people. I humbly await Your Excellency’s command.” Cai Jing was overjoyed on hearing this. He appointed Xuan Zan as his envoy, supplied him with official documents and horses, and sent him racing through the night to Pudong to invite Guan Sheng with due ceremony to the capital for deliberations. The assembled officials then withdrew.

p.src: We need not burden the tale with needless detail. Xuan Zan took the documents, mounted his horse, and set out. Taking three or five attendants with him, he reached the Pudong Patrol Inspector’s Office in no more than a day and dismounted before its gate. That day Guan Sheng was in his office with Hao Siwen, discussing the rise and fall of states through the ages. When he heard that an envoy had arrived from the Eastern Capital, Guan Sheng hurried out with Hao Siwen to welcome him. After exchanging courtesies, they invited him into the hall and took their seats. Guan Sheng asked, “My old friend, we have not seen each other for many years. What brings you all this way in person today?” Xuan Zan replied, “The bandits of Liangshan Marsh are attacking Beijing. Before the Grand Preceptor, I personally vouched that you possess strategies capable of pacifying the realm and talents fit to subdue armies and slay their commanders. By special command of the court and on the Grand Preceptor’s express orders, I have brought ceremonial silks and horses to invite you formally to depart. You must not decline, brother. Please make ready at once and come to the capital.” Guan Sheng was delighted to hear this and said to Xuan Zan, “This brother’s surname is Hao and his given names are Siwen. He and I are sworn brothers. Before his birth, his mother dreamed that the celestial beast Well-Wood Wild Dog descended into her womb, after which she conceived and bore him; hence men call him ‘Well-Wood Wild Dog.’ There is not one of the eighteen forms of martial skill that this brother has not mastered. Since the Grand Preceptor has deigned to summon me, what objection could there be to his going with us, so that together we may serve the realm?” Xuan Zan gladly agreed and urged them to set out at once.

p.src: Guan Sheng then gave instructions to his household. Together with Hao Siwen, he gathered more than ten men from west of the passes, prepared their blades, horses, armor, and baggage, and followed Xuan Zan through the night. On reaching the Eastern Capital, they went directly to the Grand Preceptor’s residence and dismounted before the gate. The gatekeeper reported their arrival to Grand Preceptor Cai, who ordered them admitted. Xuan Zan led Guan Sheng and Hao Siwen directly to the council chamber. After making their obeisance, they stood below the steps. Cai Jing looked upon Guan Sheng and saw a man of truly imposing appearance: a stately figure of eight feet five or six inches, three slender wisps of beard, brows sweeping into his temples, phoenix eyes tilted upward, a face like a dark-red date, and lips as though painted with vermilion. The Grand Preceptor was delighted and asked, “How many years have you seen, General?” Guan Sheng replied, “I am thirty-two.” Grand Preceptor Cai said, “The bandits of Liangshan Marsh have surrounded the city of Beijing. I ask you, able commander, to devise a brilliant stratagem and raise the siege.” Guan Sheng submitted, “I have long heard that these bandits have occupied the marsh and gathered a great rabble, stirring up disorder. Now they have left their lair of their own accord and thereby invited disaster upon themselves. To relieve Beijing directly would only squander manpower. I beg to be granted several tens of thousands of elite troops. I shall first seize Liangshan and then capture the bandits, leaving them unable to attend to both head and tail.” The Grand Preceptor was overjoyed at these words and said to Xuan Zan, “This is the stratagem of besieging Wei to rescue Zhao. It accords perfectly with my own thought.” He immediately summoned the officials of the Bureau of Military Affairs and had fifteen thousand elite troops from Shandong and Hebei assigned to the expedition. Hao Siwen was appointed vanguard, Xuan Zan commander of the rear guard, and Guan Sheng commander-in-chief of the army, while Grand Commandant of Infantry Duan Chang was charged with supporting them with provisions and fodder. After rewarding the three armies, he ordered them to depart by a fixed date. Brandishing great blades and broad axes, they drove fiercely toward Liangshan Marsh. Thus was the dragon drawn from the great sea, no longer able to ride the mist and soar among the clouds; and once the tiger came down to the level plain, how could it bare its fangs and flourish its claws? Truly, while coveting the mid-autumn moon in heaven, one loses the hall-illuminating pearl upon one’s plate. What fate ultimately befell Song Jiang’s army will be revealed in the next chapter.
